meta.title: Chest pain in the arvo
learning_objectives: Take a focused chest pain history using SOCRATES
Recognise features of acute coronary syndrome and exclude dangerous mimics
Outline immediate ED investigation and management of suspected ACS
references: NHFA/CSANZ Australian Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Acute Coronary Syndromes 2016

case.candidate_brief: You are an intern in the Emergency Department of a metropolitan hospital in Melbourne. Michael Nguyen, 58, has presented with chest pain this afternoon. Triage observations: HR 96, BP 152/90, RR 20, SpO2 96% on room air, T 36.8°C. Take a history, then present your findings to the examiner.
case.assessment_task: Present your history, your differential diagnoses, and your initial investigations and management.

patient.name: Michael Nguyen
patient.occupation: Owns and runs a bakery in Footscray
patient.background: Vietnamese-Australian, born in Melbourne. Married, two adult children.
patient.persona_notes: Worried and a bit breathless. Talks quickly, asks 'is it serious?' more than once. Settles noticeably if the student explains what they are doing and reassures him he is in the right place.
patient.opening_statement: I've got this awful tightness in my chest, doctor. It started a couple of hours ago at work and it just won't go away.

presenting_complaint.site: Centre of the chest, behind the breastbone
presenting_complaint.onset: Came on about 2 hours ago while lifting sacks of flour at the bakery
presenting_complaint.character: Tight and heavy, 'like someone sitting on my chest'
presenting_complaint.radiation: Down the left arm and up into the jaw
presenting_complaint.associated: Sweaty, nauseated, a bit short of breath
presenting_complaint.timing: Constant since it started; hasn't eased with rest
presenting_complaint.exacerbating_relieving: Nothing makes it better; worse when he walked in from the car park

facts.content: It's a tight, heavy feeling right in the middle of my chest.
It came on about two hours ago when I was lifting flour sacks at work.
It goes down my left arm, and my jaw aches too.
I was dripping with sweat and I feel like I might be sick.
It hasn't gone away even though I've been sitting down for ages.
It's about a seven out of ten.
I'm a bit short of breath, yeah.
For the last couple of weeks I've had a tightness when I carry stuff at work, but it went away after a few minutes rest. It's been happening more often.
No, it's not tearing and it doesn't go through to my back.
No leg swelling or pain, and I haven't been on any long trips.
Breathing in doesn't make it worse, and leaning forward doesn't change it.
No fever, no cough.
I've got type 2 diabetes, about eight years now.
My GP says my blood pressure is high.
High cholesterol too.
I take metformin 1 gram twice a day and perindopril 5 milligrams in the morning.
I was on atorvastatin but I stopped it about six months ago because my muscles ached.
Penicillin gives me a rash.
I smoke about a pack a day, since I was about twenty.
A couple of beers on the weekend, that's it.
I start at the bakery at 4am. My wife's at home, I'll need to call her.
My dad died of a heart attack when he was 60.
I keep thinking about my dad. I'm scared it's my heart.
Who's going to run the shop tomorrow? We've got big orders.

ice.ideas: Thinks it might be his heart, like his father
ice.concerns: Dying like his dad; who will run the bakery
ice.expectations: Wants to be told it's not serious and go home, but will accept staying if it's explained

behaviour_rules: Asks 'Is it serious, doctor?' if the student goes quiet or doesn't explain what they're doing
Becomes calmer and more forthcoming once the student acknowledges his worry
Does not understand medical jargon; asks what a term means if the student uses one

clinical.diagnosis: Acute coronary syndrome (likely NSTEMI) on a background of crescendo angina

differentials.discriminating_features: Exertional onset, central heavy pain radiating to arm and jaw, diaphoresis, ongoing at rest, crescendo pattern, multiple risk factors
Tearing pain radiating to the back, pulse or BP differential. Pain not tearing, no back radiation
Pleuritic pain, haemoptysis, DVT signs, immobility. None present
Sharp pain relieved by sitting forward, recent viral illness. Absent
Burning, meal-related, relieved by antacids. Diagnosis of exclusion here

red_flags.why: Radiation to arm and jaw is typical of myocardial ischaemia
Autonomic features suggest a high-risk ischaemic event
Ongoing ischaemic pain at rest needs immediate ECG and treatment
Crescendo angina indicates unstable coronary disease

expected_investigations: 12-lead ECG within 10 minutes of arrival, repeated if pain persists or changes
Serial high-sensitivity troponin per local ACS pathway
FBC, UEC, LFT, lipids, glucose and HbA1c, coagulation profile
expected_management: Manage in a monitored bed; IV access
Aspirin 300 mg orally (no aspirin allergy; penicillin allergy is irrelevant)
Sublingual GTN for ongoing pain if SBP > 90 mmHg; IV opioid analgesia if pain persists
Risk stratify (e.g. GRACE) and discuss with the cardiology registrar early; consider antithrombotic therapy and coronary angiography per guideline
Address modifiable risk factors before discharge: smoking cessation, statin re-challenge, diabetes and BP control
safety_netting: Explains he needs to stay for monitoring and tests
Tells staff immediately if pain worsens, or if he feels faint or more breathless

examiner_question_bank.question: What would you be looking for on his ECG, and what would you do if you saw ST elevation?
Which features in this history make an aortic dissection less likely?
He mentions he stopped his statin. How would you address that before discharge?
What risk stratification tools could help guide his management?

items.label: Characterises the pain (site, onset, character, radiation, severity, timing)
Asks about associated symptoms (sweating, nausea, breathlessness)
Identifies the crescendo pattern of prior exertional pain
Elicits cardiovascular risk factors (diabetes, hypertension, cholesterol, smoking, family history)
Takes a medication and allergy history, including the stopped statin
Screens for dangerous mimics (dissection, PE, pericarditis)
Explores his fear about his heart and his worry about the bakery
Gives acute coronary syndrome as the leading diagnosis
Considers aortic dissection and PE as must-not-miss differentials, with reasons
Requests serial hs-troponin and appropriate bloods
Gives aspirin, analgesia/GTN, oxygen only if hypoxic, and monitoring
Addresses secondary prevention (smoking, statin, diabetes, BP)
Treats this as a time-critical presentation
